title: Liu Xiu Burns the Letters
text:
In the chaos that followed the fall of Wang Mang's short-lived dynasty, several men fought to restore or replace the Han. In 24 AD Liu Xiu, a member of the Han imperial clan, besieged the city of Handan, held by his rival Wang Lang, a pretender who claimed to be a Han prince.

When Handan fell and Wang Lang was killed, Liu Xiu's men seized the enemy's archives. Among them, according to the official History of the Later Han, were thousands of letters from officials and officers on Liu Xiu's own side, writing to Wang Lang to curry favor with him or to slander Liu Xiu while the outcome was uncertain.

Liu Xiu did not read them. He gathered his generals, had the letters burned in front of them, and said it was so that those who were uneasy could set their minds at rest.

No one was punished for what he had once written. The following year Liu Xiu proclaimed himself emperor as Guangwu of Han. He reunited China and is remembered as one of the most capable and generous founders of a Chinese dynasty.
lesson: Sometimes the wisest thing is not to look for every past disloyalty. Letting people put a moment of weakness behind them can earn their lasting loyalty.
people: Liu Xiu (Emperor Guangwu of Han), Wang Lang
source: Fan Ye, Book of the Later Han (Hou Hanshu), Annals of Emperor Guangwu
